extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of German literature; literary critics; poets and writers studying literary history and criticism
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for assessing and understanding German poets, dramatists, and philosophers — how epoch, form, language, and philosophical temper affect literary quality. Emphasizes what to value and avoid when judging or producing poetry, drama, and literary criticism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Philosophical_inspiration_aligned_with_subject
rubrics_metrics.description: Philosophical tendencies (e.g., Platonism) can harmonize with a love of art but, if excessively strong, may lift the writer 'very far above the subjects of which he treated.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Winkelmann's Platonic inspiration provided high ideas of art but sometimes carried him beyond appropriate subject-matter; caution that a dominating philosophical bent can make treatment unsuitable to the topic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guard_against_excessive_enthusiasm_and_reverie
rubrics_metrics.description: Enthusiasm and reveries may be inspiring but must be guarded; excessive enthusiasm leads to mistakes that are easily discovered and ridiculed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author cautions that even masterly learning (Leibnitz) and sound judgment (Lessing) could not prevent errors born of enthusiasm; anti-pattern: unchecked 'physiognomical reveries' or dreamy speculation that obscure truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate_authors_in_historical_and_epochal_context
rubrics_metrics.description: The external circumstances and ruling spirit of the epoch in which a writer is educated and develops frequently determine the character of his genius and exert decisive influence on his choice of subjects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the generational framework (first/second/third generation) to interpret tendencies, e.g., revolutionary period produced different themes and energies; do not judge works divorced from their historical milieu.

rubrics_metrics.name: Revolutionary_periods_favor_invention_over_polish
rubrics_metrics.description: Periods of convulsion (revolutionary epochs) tend to favor invention and creative energy rather than perfect finishing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expectation: more invention than finish, though some works (e.g., by Schiller) can combine both; when judging works from such periods, weight should be given to imaginative breadth and vigor even if formal finish is imperfect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance_invention_with_judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: Ambition should be to perfect what has been begun — not to show invention at the expense of judgment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid valuing novelty alone; the text warns against a 'new school' that prizes invention over sound judgment and advises striving for completion and refinement as well as originality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetic_art_and_beauty_of_language
rubrics_metrics.description: High poetic quality is measured by poetical art and beauty of language as well as by thought and subject-matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Goethe's maturer works are praised for poetical art and beauty of language; assess both conceptual depth and linguistic excellence when evaluating poetry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form_must_fit_poet's_nature_and_subject
rubrics_metrics.description: The choice of form (dramatic, epic, romantic) should suit the poet's nature and the subject; a mismatch diminishes effectiveness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Goethe often leans toward the romantic/epic sphere; Schiller is fundamentally a dramatic poet. Evaluate whether a work's form (epic vs drama vs romantic) plays to the author's strengths.

rubrics_metrics.name: Harmony_between_poetry_and_stage_suitability
rubrics_metrics.description: There should be harmony between a dramatic poem and its suitability for representation on the stage; some dramas are composed not for performance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: writing dramas that never intended for representation (Klopstock, some Goethe pieces) can reveal a disconnect with theatrical demands; Schiller is praised for giving the German drama a proper sphere and form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Internal_harmony_of_authorial_spirit
rubrics_metrics.description: A writer's internal harmony (mental unity, settled principle) significantly affects the emotional tone and success of his works; pervasive doubt or scepticism can chill them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Schiller's persistent doubts produce an 'internal coldness' that tempers even his noblest works; assess whether the author's intellectual temperament supports or undermines artistic expression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid_narrow_imitation_of_the_antique
rubrics_metrics.description: Imitating antiquity or great predecessors on narrow principles is a defect; writers should borrow the best parts rather than slavishly copy forms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The imitation of the antique conducted on narrow principles is criticized; preference is given to judicious adoption and creative transformation over mere imitation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity_and_purity_of_language_in_philosophical_writing
rubrics_metrics.description: Philosophical prose should aim for purity and clarity; obfuscated or cipher terminology is a 'barbarism' that hinders understanding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kant's 'unfortunate Terminology' is cited as an example; the best recent philosophical writings are praised for being 'quite pure in respect of language.' Avoid convoluted jargon and coinages that mask meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Place_of_reason_and_experience_in_philosophical_claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Reason alone is insufficient to decide matters of moral and divine import; true knowledge of divine things must be grounded in experience and facts of human life rather than pure speculative reason.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critique of Kant: he 'erroneously assigned [reason] the first' place. For philosophical writing that addresses religion or morality, prioritize empirical grounding and experience-informed argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate_moral_tendency_of_literary_works
rubrics_metrics.description: The moral tendency of literary works matters: works that promote a merely Epicurean (pleasure-centered) morality have a dangerous tendency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wieland's philosophical romances are noted as promoting an Epicurean system and judged as having a 'dangerous tendency'; consider ethical consequences and orientations when assessing literature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account_for_public_engagement_and_audience_influence
rubrics_metrics.description: The size and character of the public/readership shape literature; revolutionary changes in readership affect what writers produce and how works are received.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Revolution expanded readership and public interest; the author predicts literature will become less the concern of individuals and more of the public, so evaluate works in light of their intended and actual audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid_sectarianism_and_value_synthesis
rubrics_metrics.description: Sectarian spirit and rigid party forms are defects; a milder, less sectarian approach that prepares various parties to work together is preferable for intellectual progress.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The decline of sectarianism (Illuminati, Kantians splitting) is seen as positive; in criticism and composition, avoid narrow sectarian positions and seek elements of truth across schools.
